17 AI System Concepts Every Founder Should Understand Before Hiring an AI Agency

A founder once sent me an agency proposal that used 16 of these 17 terms. It did not contain a single number. The 1 term it skipped was evaluations.

Founders read charts like this as a shopping list. I read them as a bill of materials. Every box is something you pay for, maintain, and get blamed for when it breaks in front of a customer. Here is how I break it down.

4 of these boxes decide whether you have a product. Embeddings, vector databases, RAG, and context engineering. This is the part everyone demos. Getting it 80% right takes a week. The last 15% takes months, and that 15% is where your customer decides whether to trust it.

3 of them decide whether you have a business. Semantic caching, model routing, and an AI gateway. None of them show up in a demo, and together they set your gross margin. I once audited a product that lost money on every paying user because every question, including "what are your opening hours," went to the largest model available. Routing and caching fixed it in 2 weeks and cut inference spend by more than half.

5 of them decide how much risk you carry. Function calling, tool use, MCP, external integrations, and the agent harness. This is where AI starts writing to your CRM, sending emails, touching money. Every capability you hand an agent is a liability until you can prove how it behaves. My month 1 default: the agent drafts, a person approves.

3 of them decide whether it still works in month 6. The execution loop, memory, and guardrails. Most agent failures I get called in to fix live here. A loop that never terminates. Memory that leaks 1 customer's context into another's session. Guardrails added after a bad answer reached a client.

And 2 of them decide whether the other 15 are real. Observability and evaluations. If an agency cannot show you a test set, a baseline score, and a trace of every request in the first 2 weeks, you have no way to know what you are paying for.

So the most useful question to ask any agency is which of the 17 they would leave out, and why. Most products I scope need 8 to 10. Some need a classifier and a well-written SQL query, and I tell founders that on the first call, even when it shrinks my contract.

That is also why clients stay with me for years. From week 1, they own the evaluation set, the dashboards, and the cost per query. After that, every decision is based on numbers they can see, so the work shifts from building the system to growing it.

I am Muhammad Ghulam Jillani, Founder and CEO at Jillani SofTech. 22+ production AI systems across Healthcare, Finance, Legal, and SaaS.

Planning an AI product, or holding an agency proposal you doubt? Book 30 minutes with me today, free. Bring the plan or the proposal. You leave knowing which of the 17 you need, which ones are missing, and what the build should cost.

There is a new funding opportunity coming to Vienna this autumn that I think founders should watch, especially if you are already beyond the idea/early-startup stage and are trying to finance the next serious step.

So, the City of Vienna and Raiffeisen-Holding Lower Austria-Vienna are launching “Wiener Wachstum”, a new financing instrument with an initial €7M budget. The first financings are planned for 2027, while application details have not yet been published and are expected to be announced as the programme launches this autumn.

€100K–€500K per financing round

The instrument is designed for growth-oriented SMEs that already have a business and need additional equity to expand.
According to the City of Vienna, financing can be used for entering new markets, investing in technology, hiring, increasing production capacity, business acquisitions and management buy-outs.
The agreed financing amount is paid out in full. Unlike a traditional grant, a share of the profit is returned to Wiener Wachstum, creating a revolving financing model that can support additional companies later.
I think this distinction matters.
If you are looking for €20K to validate an idea, this probably isn't the instrument you are waiting for. But if you already have traction and your next bottleneck is capital for expansion, €100K–€500K becomes much more relevant.

Which startups are actually in focus?

The programme targets future-oriented sectors, including:
• Life Sciences
• MedTech
• Pharma
• Diagnostics
• Software
• AI
• Quantum technologies
• Cybersecurity
• IT services
And there is another detail I find particularly interesting: internationalisation is explicitly listed as a use case.
That makes the instrument potentially interesting for a Vienna company that has proven its product locally but now needs capital to enter Germany, another European market or a larger international market.

The City says the programme is designed to address a financing gap faced by established SMEs at the point where they move into their next growth phase.
The initial €7M will be provided equally by Wirtschaftsagentur Wien and Raiffeisen-Holding NÖ-Wien.

What should founders do now?

If your company could fit the programme, I would already have three things ready:
1. A clear growth plan — what exactly happens after the financing?
2. A concrete capital allocation — technology, hiring, market expansion, production, etc.
3. Evidence that the business is already working — revenue, customers, contracts, partnerships or other traction.
And keep an eye on the official application announcement!

I’m thrilled to share that I successfully completed the Agentic AI Hackathon '26 organized by Product Space! 🚀 

Over the weekend, Dhruthi Salankimatt and I built HireFlow, an autonomous "white-box" candidate screening agent. We wanted to solve a core issue with AI in recruiting: a lack of trust and auditability. Hiring managers don't want a black-box chatbot that just summarizes PDFs; they need to know exactly why an AI scored a candidate a certain way.
Instead of just wrapping a basic prompt in a UI, we engineered a resilient, multi-agent system using CrewAI, Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Streamlit.

My biggest technical takeaway as a developer? LLMs hallucinate, mess up date math, and crash when external APIs fail. To solve this, I built strict Pydantic data contracts and deterministic Python guardrails around our agents. If the AI invented a quote or hallucinated a metric, the code caught it, logged it, and kept the pipeline moving without crashing. During our final load test, our backend successfully caught and filtered 21 LLM hallucinations before they ever reached the UI. 📱 

The real reward was the intense engineering experience. A huge shoutout to Product Space for hosting such a challenging and forward-thinking hackathon!

The cheapest thing in property is an opinion. The most expensive is finding out what it costs...

The cheap kind has never run short. Change the unit mix. Hold it. Sell it. Refurbish it. Build the second phase. Don't build the second phase. Every one of them arrives with the confidence of a man whose name is not on the guarantee.

You know him. Far end of the committee table, has never opened the model, has a cousin in hospitality. Call him Mr Have You Considered. Have you considered a hotel component. Have you considered branded residences. Have you considered padel, habibi. Everyone's doing padel.

Finding out what his idea does to the money is expensive, so nobody finds out. The analyst nods, writes it down, and the note dies in an email thread between the QS and the weekend. Then comes the sentence every bad decision hides behind. We didn't have time to model that. Not that the question was bad. That answering it cost more than ignoring it.

Ignoring it is getting dearer. JLL and MIT Sloan School of Management have set out four paths for what AI does to employment. In one firms grow without hiring at the old rate. In another the jobs move city and leave you, in JLL's words, with wrong offices, wrong locations, wrong roles. In a third the economy looks fine while the tenant in your building needs less of it, and a long lease hides that until it doesn't. American tech employment is down 1.5 percent this year. Nearly 30 percent of San Francisco's leasing since 2025 came from AI companies. Both are true at once, and only one is in your model.

A different tenant mix changes the works, the void and the cash you put in. Phasing changes when the money leaves and how much freedom you keep if demand moves. Nobody ran either before the contracts were signed. There wasn't time.

The excuse held because both halves were true. Answering was expensive, ignoring was cheap. JLL just moved the second half. Here is what moves the first.

The useful AI is not the one in the demo reel. It sits between that pile of opinions and a proper calculation engine. It turns a question into a model change you can inspect, so more combinations get run. Mr Have You Considered gets his hotel run in the room, in the same file, on the same assumptions as everything else. You still decide. The maths still has to stand up, and probabilities still need evidence. A chatbot feeling quite confident about next year's leasing market is not evidence.

And yes, scenario analysis existed before OpenAI. Nobody is claiming Silicon Valley invented "what if". The difference is doing more of it in the fortnight before the board pack goes out.

Sometimes you come back to the original plan. Fine. It ought to survive a little competition. Sometimes the smaller intervention wins, and somebody can prove it. And every so often the hotel works, and Mr Have You Considered gets his told you so, with the numbers attached.

Opinions were always cheap. Now the answers are too. Yalla, run the hotel!

30,000 infected devices. 7,000 drained crypto wallets. $10.7 million gone. All from a job interview.


A joint advisory from the FBI, Japan NPA, Australia cyber authorities and Germany BND just named the group behind it: WaterPlum, also known as Contagious Interview. Between December 2025 and July 2026, they ran fake recruiter campaigns across 100+ countries, posing as AI, crypto and NFT companies. The pitch was always the same: attractive role, friendly chat, then a "coding test" or demo repo to run locally. That file was the malware.

What gets me isn't the tooling. It's the target selection. These weren't random phishing blasts. They went after developers, the exact people holding keys to wallets, repos and infra. And once a device is infected, the blast radius isn't just one person's crypto. It's every company that developer touches next.

We talk a lot in this industry about smart contract audits and exchange security. This is a reminder that the softest target is still a human being replying to a promising DM. No audit fixes that.

If you're hiring or job hunting in Web3 right now, verify the recruiter before you verify the offer.

70 percent of UK homecare agencies are now using or piloting AI.

Of those re-inspected since adopting it, 59 percent saw their CQC rating go up. Not one saw it drop.

Read that again. In a sector where operators spend the year worrying about the next inspection, one technology decision is quietly moving the needle in one direction only.

Here is the awkward bit though. When those same providers were asked how clear current CQC guidance on AI is, they scored it around 2 out of 4. Half a sector piloting something the regulator has only just started writing rules for.

The gap between "we have a system" and "our system actually improved our care" is not the software vendor. It is the operator sitting in the chair.

Three questions worth asking before you sign the next contract.

1. What decision will this tool make faster or better? If you cannot name one in a sentence, park it.
2. Who owns the exceptions when the tool flags something? Software surfaces risk. Humans still act on it.
3. What will the tool do that your registered manager currently does on a Sunday night in a spreadsheet? That is where the hours actually get freed up.

The providers I see doing best with AI right now treat it like hiring a very fast junior. Brief it properly. Check its work. Do not let it near safeguarding decisions on its own.

The regulator will catch up. The operators who worked it out first will already have the evidence when they do.

What is one thing you would automate this quarter if you knew CQC would smile on it?

Recent figures from Denmark's Nationalbank show that companies using #AI are hiring 9-11% fewer people, epecially young workers and those with higher education. 

The figures should give rise to great concern. If start level jobs are being automated, how will young people ever gain the skills needed to learn, grow and progress in the labour market? What gaps are we creating as cohorts retire and experience disappears? What about the future financing of pensions, the welfare state? What about the economy? And not least how will this affect the young economically, socially and psychologically? 

Technology driven unemployment is not a new thing. But the widespread use of AI across all sectors will mean that employment will be affected across most occupations. The report from the Nationalbank states that 59% of Danish companies are already using AI. We can only expect that figure to rise. Whilst unemployment levels have not risen yet, can we expect them to? If so, then what for the young workers?

And what about the workers with higher education? Given that higher education is free in Denmark, we must ask whether the state is financing an unsustainable future? Who bears the responsibility? What will be the consequences of rising unemployment, a decline in buying power, less tax revenue and the resulting socio-economic changes? Technologies don't pay tax. Who then, will pay for the welfare state's continuation? And if the welfare state collapses, what then?

Many many questions and as of yet few concrete answers. We only need to look at countries with high youth unemployment to see how deep the crisis can go. China with 19% youth unemployment. South Africa 60%. 

Do we need a new social contract that obliges companies to hire new cohorts? How do we maintain quality jobs and decent working conditions if the competition for a job, any job, rises? 

What is the responsibility of older generations who have benefitted from economic growth and the universal welfare state towards the generations that follow? It no longer seems plausible that we can sit back and let the market  determine the future.

Our org charts may be describing yesterday’s jobs.

One of the most interesting AI findings I read this week has little to do with #productivity.
OpenAI’s latest economic research suggests that people are increasingly using AI to perform tasks that traditionally belonged to other occupations ( 👉 https://lnkd.in/eAC9Himv)

That may sound incremental. I think it could become a major ORGANIATIONAL SHIFT.
Across #banking, #telecom, #technology and #infrastructure, we’ve built organizations around specialization — for good reasons.

But AI is making the edges between roles cheaper to cross.

 🔥 A finance professional can prototype an analysis.
 🔥 An engineer can interrogate contracts.
 🔥 A business expert can build a small tool.

And suddenly, the question changes.
⚡ What happens when people can evolve their jobs faster than we can redesign them?
That has implications far beyond tool adoption:
→ Role definitions
→ Team composition
→ Career paths
→ Decision rights
→ Hiring profiles
#Expertise still matters. Probably more than ever.
But the future organization may be less about protecting functional boundaries — and more about #enabling people to move across them safely and effectively.

💡 The real opportunity may not be automating today’s job descriptions.
It may be expanding what people are able to do.
